title: Virtually a drug scare: Mephedrone and the impact of the internet on drug news transmission

claims.statement: In the UK mephedrone scare of 2009–2010, several deaths that online news linked to mephedrone were later reported not to have been caused by it, including the deaths most linked to it online; the evidence is one study of online news whose later toxicology comes second-hand from press reports of inquests, so its figures are illustrative. Searching Google News from 26 November 2009 to one year after the ban (enforced on 16 April 2010), the author found 18 named people whose deaths online news linked to mephedrone; suicides and violent or accidental deaths were left out, and their number is not given. Later press reports said that mephedrone was not found in 4, including two young men in Scunthorpe, whose names were linked to mephedrone on about 9,060 and 8,730 web pages by June 2011 (more than any other case), who were reported a month after the ban not to have taken mephedrone, and whose inquest in 2011 found that they died from alcohol combined with methadone; that it was found but was not a factor in 4; and that it was a factor in 7, six of them with other drugs or illnesses also alleged. For 3 there was no later toxicology note, and the first death linked to mephedrone, of a 14-year-old girl in November 2009, was reported in local news within a month as due to natural causes (pneumonia after a streptococcal infection), yet went on being named as a mephedrone death in local, national and international news for months. The author reads the volume of news as showing that reports confirming that mephedrone was not responsible were far fewer than the earlier reports suggesting that it was. Relative Google searches for 'mephedrone', and for 'mephedrone buy', rose around the most-reported deaths and fell after the ban; these are screenshots of relative search volume without numbers, and the author concedes that a search is not a purchase, so they do not show that the news made people seek or use the drug (Forsyth, 2012). For comparison, the paper cites official statistics recording 6 drug-related deaths involving mephedrone, confirmed by toxicology, among 2,747 drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 2010, 2 of them with mephedrone as the only drug found (as cited by Forsyth, 2012). The 18 deaths are the media's selection, not a count of deaths involving mephedrone, and the outcome of each comes from newspapers rather than coroners' records; how many deaths blamed on mephedrone were confirmed in national registers is in the answer on confirmed mephedrone deaths. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Forsyth (2012), 18 named deaths linked to mephedrone in online news (26 November 2009 to about April 2011; suicides and violent or accidental deaths excluded, number not given). Later press reports: not detected 4; detected, not a factor 4; detected and a factor 7 (6 with other drugs or conditions alleged); no toxicology note 3 (one reported as natural causes); editors' tally of Table 1 notes. Most-linked cases: 9,060 and 8,730 web pages (Scunthorpe; alcohol and methadone at inquest). Cited from ONS: 6 toxicologically confirmed mephedrone-related deaths among 2,747 drug-related deaths, England and Wales, 2010; mephedrone the only drug in 2. Search data relative only, no numbers.
